parsed.summary: The Lean theorem asserts that some finitely presented group G is not sofic. Soficity is the standard local definition: for every finite F ⊆ G and every 0<ε<1 there is a map G → Sym(n), n>0, with σ(1)=1, that is ε-multiplicative on F and moves almost all points for each nontrivial g ∈ F. The definitions look faithful. The main caveat: the Lean statement is a bare existential and never names L_{F2}(1,2)^×, so it does not formalize Theorem 1.1 as stated. It instead adds finite presentability, which the excerpt does not mention.

glossary.plain: d_H(p,q) = |{y : p(y) ≠ q(y)}| / |Y| for permutations p, q of a finite set Y
glossary.note: Division by 0 occurs only for empty Y. Every use is on Fin size with size > 0.

glossary.plain: A positive integer n together with a map σ: G → Sym(n) satisfying σ(1)=1
glossary.standard_concept: a map G → Sym(n) used in a sofic approximation
glossary.note: The extra condition σ(1)=1 is harmless. Resetting σ(1) to 1 can only improve the approximation inequalities.

glossary.plain: For all g,h ∈ F: d_H(σ(gh), σ(g)σ(h)) < ε. For all g ∈ F with g ≠ 1: d_H(σ(g), 1) > 1 − ε.
For every finite F ⊆ G and every 0 < ε < 1 there exists an (F,ε)-good permutation model
glossary.note: Restricting to ε < 1 is harmless, since smaller ε is the harder case.

lean_claims.plain: There exists a group G (in Type 0) that is finitely presented (Mathlib's Group.IsFinitelyPresented) and is not sofic in the above sense.

paper_claims.plain: The unit group of the binary Leavitt algebra L_{F2}(1,2) is not sofic.

coverage.why: Lean only asserts that some finitely presented nonsofic group exists; it does not identify the group as L_{F2}(1,2)^×. Finite presentability of that unit group (or any fp corollary) is not in the excerpt.

flags.explanation: The paper states nonsoficity of a specific group, L_{F2}(1,2)^×. The Lean theorem is an existential over all groups and does not certify that the Leavitt unit group is nonsofic. It also requires finite presentability, which is not claimed in the excerpt; this may correspond to a corollary elsewhere in the paper (not in excerpt). In that respect Lean is stronger, but it is not a formalization of Theorem 1.1 as stated.
flags.probe_idea: Construct the Leavitt algebra as a quotient of FreeAlgebra (ZMod 2) (Fin 4) by the relations in (1). Then state ¬ SoficGroups.Sofic (Units R) and Group.IsFinitelyPresented (Units R) separately.

flags.explanation: The definition adds σ(1)=1 and restricts to ε<1, which looks slightly nonstandard. It is equivalent to the usual definition because both changes only make approximations easier to find or are achievable without loss. Since the theorem negates Sofic, extra constraints in GoodOn would make the Lean claim weaker; here they are harmless.
flags.probe_idea: Prove Sofic G ↔ the standard definition without map_one and with all ε > 0.

lint_verdicts.why: The definition is only applied to Fin size with size_pos, so the denominator is nonzero.
ε is a real number, so 1 − ε is real subtraction and does not truncate.
